nameStory: The 'tailed' in this spider's name comes from its distinctly squarish abdomen that extends backward like a little tail when viewed from the side. Combined with its preference for dark, damp spaces like cellars and basements, it earned the descriptive name 'tailed cellar spider.' Some folks also call them 'box spiders' because of that squared-off rear end!
description: The Tailed Cellar Spider is a delicate house guest with incredibly long, thin legs that can stretch up to 2.4 inches across - nearly five times longer than its tiny body! Their most distinctive feature is a squarish abdomen that looks like a small box attached to their round front section. These fragile-looking spiders have six eyes arranged in pairs and prefer to hang out in the quiet corners of our homes, where they build messy webs to catch flying insects.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is distinctly square or box-like when viewed from the side, while the front section (cephalothorax) appears circular from above - like a tiny box attached to a button

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length ranges from just 2.5-7mm (smaller than your pinky nail), but those thread-like legs can span up to 6cm across - they feel as delicate as spider silk when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Six small, dark eyes arranged in three pairs - fewer than most spiders you'll encounter, giving them a distinctive facial pattern

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates loose, irregular webs that look messy and abandoned compared to classic orb webs - they feel sticky but flimsy when accidentally walked through

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in its web and vibrates rapidly when disturbed, creating a blur of motion that makes it nearly impossible to see clearly

habitat: Look for Tailed Cellar Spiders in the quiet, undisturbed corners of human structures throughout New England - basements, cellars, garages, sheds, and crawl spaces are their favorites. They prefer areas with consistent moisture and minimal air movement, often building webs near water heaters, in window wells, or along foundation walls. You'll rarely find them outdoors, as they've adapted specifically to living alongside humans in our buildings.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, expanding their webs and beginning courtship behaviors in basements and cellars.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with the most visible web-building and hunting. Look for them in cool basement corners during hot days.
seasonality.fall: Mating season brings males wandering more openly. Egg sacs may be visible as small, loosely wrapped bundles in webs.
seasonality.winter: Remain active year-round in heated buildings, though they may be less mobile during coldest periods. Webs often accumulate more dust and debris.

funFact: Tailed Cellar Spiders have two different types of sound-producing organs and can actually make noise - though it's too quiet for human ears to detect without special equipment!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other daddy longlegs, but remember: if it has a web and a boxy abdomen, it's the tailed cellar spider. True daddy longlegs (harvestmen) don't make webs and have pill-shaped bodies, while other cellar spiders have round or oval abdomens.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'daddy longlegs spiders,' they're not closely related to the creatures most people call daddy longlegs (which aren't actually spiders at all, but harvestmen). This naming confusion leads many people to mix up several completely different arachnids that just happen to have long, thin legs.
compareHints: The Tailed Cellar Spider is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among local cellar spiders. Compared to other cellar spider family members like the Long-bodied Cellar Spider, it's distinguished by that characteristic square abdomen and slightly more robust appearance. Other cellar spiders in the region have elongated oval or cylindrical abdomens, never that distinctive boxy shape.
